newsitem.title: CHINA: HK business seeks magic behind Tung's words.
newsitem.headline: HK business seeks magic behind Tung's words.

text.p: Tung Chee-hwa's pledge to make Hong Kong's economy more competitive failed to surprise business leaders on Wednesday, but some asked the territory's new leader to reveal "the magic behind the words."
"This is pretty much what you'd expect for a politician coming in with a lot of promises but short on detail," said Kent Rossiter, head of institutional sales for Nikko Securities.
"I hate to be negative, but I don't see a lot of magic behind the words."

In a policy speech made just hours after Hong Kong returned to Chinese control on Tuesday, Tung took aim at nearly all the issues hampering the territory's competitiveness while declaring his determination to ensure it remained "the world's freest and most vibrant economy".
Education, property, high technology, languages and social issues all fell under the spotlight as Tung outlined his vision of the new Hong Kong.

"If he succeeds in fulfilling three quarters of the pledges in his first speech ... (Tung's) term in office will far outclass the performance of any previous Hong Kong government. His aims are ambitious," the South China Morning Post, Hong Kong's flagship English-language newspaper, wrote on Wednesday.
Tung's promise to address Hong Kong's critical property issue was greeted particularly warmly.
For many years, exorbitant property prices have lined the pockets of a small cartel of property developers while depriving ordinary Hong Kong people of reasonable housing.
Now they are pricing Hong Kong out of the Asian market for multinational corporations seeking a regional headquarters.
Tung has promised to speed up urban redevelopment, extend the territory's mass transit system and infrastructure development and stamp out "rampant" property speculation.
He has promised to release at least 85,000 new housing units on to the market each year, raising the level of home ownership in Hong Kong to at least 70 percent within the decade.
"In principle this is the right thing to do...but it really depends on what the substance is," said Simon Ogus, chief economist with SBC Warburg.
"The government announced all sorts of things in the past and, when the details finally came out, you find out they actually have very little teeth."
None of Tung's comments should have come as a surprise, particularly his controversial interest in developing a high technology industry, said Stephen Xu, economist at Standard Chartered Bank.

"For a very long time, if you read carefully what C.H. Tung has been saying, he has been showing admiration for (Singapore's elder statesman) Lee Kuan Yew in that the government should play an important role in the economy," said Xu.
Rossiter warned it will take a great deal more than a government decree to make Hong Kong the best high-tech centre in Asia, and competition from other regional centres is fierce.
"I'm not saying this is a bad idea, I'm just saying we have a long way to go. It will take massive incentives," he said.
Despite the call for more details, Ogus said it was unfair to expect Tung to make any concrete commitments in his first speech as chief executive.
"This was largely a ceremonial address. This was not a policy-making address," he said.
Tung is expected to flesh out some of these ideas in an official policy address in October before the provisional legislature, Hong Kong's new, China-appointed parliament.
